name: eip681 differential corpus
note: Each case carries the EIP-681 rule it probes AND a `strength`. strength=spec means EIP-681 or RFC 3986 requires the answer and a mismatch is a genuine failure; strength=opinion means the spec is silent and the answer is a defensible judgement call, so a mismatch is reported for discussion and does not fail the run. Without this distinction the corpus would be asserting its author's reading as if it were the spec.

cases.rule: EIP-681 target-only form is legal. The chain is unnamed, so a wallet may resolve the address on the wrong chain.
`@chainId` names the chain.
EIP-681 states value MAY be expressed in scientific notation. This is the single most commonly mis-implemented rule.
Plain decimal integer wei.
RFC 3986 s3.1: URI schemes are case-insensitive. Rejecting 'Ethereum:' is a spec violation.
Same as above; mixed case is still the same scheme.
ERC-20 form: contract in the target, /transfer function, address= payee, uint256= base units.
The scientific-notation permission attaches to numeric arguments generally, not only to `value`.
A /transfer call with an address but no uint256 is incomplete; the amount would be undefined.
value= and an ERC-20 call carry two different amounts. Something has to pick one, silently. This is the case BTCpayServer.USDt#67 ran into.
Legal but dangerous: USDC exists at different addresses on different chains, so the contract address alone does not identify the chain.
EIP-681 defines the 'ethereum' scheme. A different scheme must be handed to a different handler, not parsed as EIP-681.
Not a URI at all in the EIP-681 sense.
Target must be 20 bytes of hex.
Too short to be an address. Accepting it means a wallet must guess.
Addresses carry the 0x prefix. Bare hex is ambiguous and must not be silently prefixed.
EIP-55 test vector #2, correctly cased. Valid.
Same address, mixed case, checksum fails. Mixed case IS a checksum claim. The dangerous middle ground: a lenient parser accepts it and pays the address anyway.
All-uppercase makes no checksum claim, so there is nothing to fail. All-lowercase likewise.
A zero-value transfer is almost always a bug at the caller. Trading implementations differ here; refusing is the safe direction.
Digit string; leading zeros do not change the value. Good canonicalisation test.
Unsigned quantity. A negative wei amount cannot be expressed.
wei is the smallest unit; fractional wei does not exist.
value is decimal in EIP-681. Accepting 0x10 as 16 (or as 10) is a divergence trap.
EIP-155 chain ids start at 1. 0 is not a chain.
Beyond Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER. A parser that returns a truncated float chain id will route payment to the wrong chain.
chainId is a decimal integer in the URI.
Two conflicting amounts. Whichever a parser picks, the other reader may pick differently.
EIP-681 allows supplementary parameters; unknown ones should be preserved or ignored, not turned into a hard failure.
Empty query. Structurally a URI with no parameters.
A bare address is not an EIP-681 URI. Treating one as the other is how a QR scanner mis-reads a plain address.
EIP-681 target is an address. ENS names are a separate concern and must not be silently resolved.
Empty input.
A /transfer with no parameters cannot specify a payee or an amount.
